Cape Canaveral, 1989-10-18. Deployed from the Space Shuttle bay above the Atlantic and boosted by the Inertial Upper Stage — the post-Challenger replacement for the originally-planned Centaur G upper stage, which had been banned from the Shuttle for safety reasons. The lower-energy IUS forced a 6-year VEEGA cruise instead of a direct 2-year transfer.

Closest approach 16,000 km from Venus on 1990-02-10. The VEEGA (Venus-Earth-Earth Gravity Assist) profile starts here, stealing orbital energy from Venus to raise Galileo's aphelion outward. The thermal load near Venus exceeded the original mission spec; engineers added insulation on the antenna boom that later kept the high-gain antenna stuck closed.

Closest approach 960 km on 1990-12-08. First of two Earth flybys; combined they will bend the trajectory enough to reach Jupiter. Galileo also returned spectral observations of Earth as a test case for life-detection methods — analysing your own planet as if from afar.

Closest approach 1,600 km from asteroid 951 Gaspra on 1991-10-29. The first close-up images of an asteroid by any spacecraft. Gaspra's irregular shape, ~20 km long, suggested it was a collision fragment from a larger parent body — confirming early Solar System collision histories.

Closest approach 304 km on 1992-12-08 — the final assist needed to reach Jupiter. Used the encounter to test the high-gain antenna deployment one more time (it would not fully open; the mission ran on the low-gain antenna for the rest of its life, requiring extensive data-compression workarounds).

Closest approach 2,400 km from asteroid 243 Ida on 1993-08-28. Discovered Ida's tiny moon Dactyl (1.4 km diameter) — the first confirmed binary asteroid system. Confirmed that asteroids could host satellites stably, reshaping models of asteroid dynamics.

Galileo's atmospheric probe separated 5 months before Jupiter arrival, on 1995-07-13, on a slightly-different ballistic trajectory targeting the giant planet's atmosphere. The probe carried no propulsion — its arrival geometry was set entirely by the separation manoeuvre.

1995-12-07. The probe entered Jupiter's atmosphere at 47.4 km/s, survived peak deceleration of 228 g, deployed a parachute, and transmitted for 58 minutes from 0.6 to 22 bar pressure before melting. Galileo simultaneously fired its main engine for 49 minutes to capture into Jupiter orbit — the first Jupiter orbiter, beginning an 8-year tour of the moons that found evidence of liquid water under Europa's ice.
First spacecraft to orbit Jupiter; atmospheric probe into Jupiter clouds

Galileo should have been crippled before it even arrived. Its main antenna stuck half-open on the way to Jupiter, cutting its data rate to a trickle — and the mission succeeded anyway, because engineers rewrote its software from Earth to squeeze the science through a tiny backup antenna. It became the first spacecraft to orbit Jupiter, dropped a probe into the giant planet’s clouds, and spent eight years touring the moons. Its greatest find emerged slowly from that persistence: the way Jupiter’s magnetic field wrapped around Europa could only be explained by a salty ocean beneath the ice — the strongest case yet that a moon of Jupiter might hold liquid water, and life. At the end it was flown into Jupiter on purpose, so it could never fall onto Europa and contaminate it.

Launched from Space Shuttle Atlantis after the long post-Challenger pause, Galileo braved the inner asteroid belt and conducted the first long-term study of Jupiter and its moons from orbit. It discovered Europa's induced magnetic field — strong evidence of a subsurface ocean — and watched Shoemaker-Levy 9 slam into Jupiter. The mission ended with a controlled plunge into Jupiter in 2003 to avoid contaminating icy moons that might harbour conditions for life.
STS-34 deploys Galileo and an inertial upper stage from Atlantis.
Main engine burn captures Galileo into orbit; an 8-year tour of moon science begins.
